title: PRINCIPALITIES AND POWERS: THE INVISIBLE WAR PAUL WARNED YOU ABOUT—AND WHY SATAN DOESN’T WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND EPHESIANS 6
paragraphs: PRINCIPALITIES AND POWERS: THE INVISIBLE WAR PAUL WARNED YOU ABOUT—AND WHY SATAN DOESN’T WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND EPHESIANS 6

Not every battle you are fighting began with another person. Not every wound is merely physical. And not every enemy can be seen. But before you blame the devil for everything going wrong in your life, you need to understand what Paul actually meant when he said, “We wrestle not against flesh and blood.” Because the truth is far more sobering—and far more hopeful—than you may have been taught.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You know what it feels like.
You wake up in the morning, reach for your phone, and before your feet even touch the floor, your mind is already fighting.
Yesterday's mistakes.
Tomorrow's uncertainties.
The temptation you promised God you would never return to.
The conversation that keeps replaying in your head.
The bitterness you thought you had forgiven.
The secret nobody at church knows about.
And somewhere beneath all that noise is a quiet, frightening question.
Why am I still struggling like this when I genuinely love Jesus?
You pray.
You read Scripture.
You worship.
You try to do better.

Yet some days, it feels as though something is pressing against your soul, trying to convince you that your faith is useless, your repentance is meaningless, and your future will never be different from your past.
Maybe you've even wondered whether God has abandoned you.
But what if the battle is not evidence that God has abandoned you?
What if Scripture has been telling us all along that following Jesus does not mean the absence of conflict?
And what if the most dangerous thing about spiritual warfare is not merely that evil exists—but that Christians can misunderstand the battle so badly that they begin fighting the wrong enemy?
That is where the apostle Paul takes us.
Not into a fantasy world where every inconvenience is a demon.
Not into a life dominated by fear of invisible beings.

But into a breathtaking revelation about the powers of darkness, the authority of Jesus Christ, and the kind of strength that can keep a wounded believer standing when everything around them is shaking.
Listen carefully to what Paul wrote:

“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.” — Ephesians 6:12, KJV
Read that again.
We wrestle not against flesh and blood.
Paul did not say that human beings never hurt us.
He did not say that injustice, abuse, betrayal, corruption, or persecution are imaginary.
He was saying something more profound.
Behind the visible conflicts of a fallen world, there is a spiritual dimension of evil that cannot be defeated by treating other human beings as our ultimate enemies.
And that changes everything.
Because the person who betrayed you is not beyond the reach of God's grace.
The family member who wounded you is not the final source of all evil.
The unbeliever who mocks your faith is not someone you have been commanded to hate.
Even the person who has made your life difficult is still a human being made in God's image.
You may need boundaries. You may need justice. You may need to confront wrongdoing or remove yourself from danger.
But you are not called to surrender your heart to hatred.
Paul is warning us that there is a greater battle than the argument happening in front of us.
And to understand that battle, we must understand his words.
When Paul wrote Ephesians, he wrote in Greek.
The phrase translated “principalities” is ἀρχάς (archas), the accusative plural of archē.
The word can refer to beginnings, rulers, or authorities, depending on its context.
Here, it refers to ruling powers or authorities within the spiritual opposition Paul is describing.
The word translated “powers” is ἐξουσίας (exousias), from exousia, meaning authority, right, or delegated power.
These words are important because Paul was not simply describing spooky figures hiding in dark corners.
He was describing a real and organized opposition to God's purposes, using language associated with rule, authority, and dominion.
Then he continues with an even more striking expression:
πρὸς τοὺς κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ σκότους τούτου
pros tous kosmokratoras tou skotous toutou
Against the world-rulers of this darkness.
The unusual Greek word kosmokratoras carries the idea of rulers exercising dominion over the world-order associated here with darkness.
But we must be careful.
Paul is not teaching that Satan owns the universe or possesses authority equal to God.
The devil is not God's opposite in power.
God has no equal.
Paul is describing the influence of evil within the present fallen order—not declaring that darkness is sovereign over creation.
Then comes the final expression:
πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις
pros ta pneumatika tēs ponērias en tois epouraniois
Against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
Notice what Paul is doing.
He is directing the attention of believers beyond merely human conflict toward spiritual opposition.
Yet he does not provide a detailed chart of demonic ranks.
He does not tell Christians to memorize the names of territorial spirits.
He does not command believers to spend their lives investigating invisible hierarchies.
Scripture does not give us enough information to build a complete organizational diagram of the demonic realm from this verse.
And we should never pretend to know more than God has revealed.
Paul's purpose is not to make us fascinated with demons.
His purpose is to make us faithful to Christ.
That distinction matters more than many Christians realize.
Because it is possible to talk about Satan constantly while speaking very little about Jesus.

It is possible to become so obsessed with spiritual warfare that every sickness becomes a curse, every disagreement becomes a demonic attack, and every difficult season becomes evidence that some invisible enemy has gained control.
But Paul never tells believers to live that way.
He begins his instructions with a command that is often overlooked.
“Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.” — Ephesians 6:10, KJV
Not strong in your ability to identify demons.
Not strong in your volume when you pray.
Not strong in your knowledge of hidden spiritual mysteries.
Strong in the Lord.
The Greek expression is ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ (endynamousthe en kyriō).
It means, in this context, to be strengthened in the Lord.
The command points believers toward strength found in their relationship with Christ and dependence upon His mighty power.
And perhaps this is exactly where some of us need to stop pretending.
Because you have been trying to fight battles that you were never meant to fight in your own strength.
You have been carrying guilt as though suffering enough could purchase forgiveness.
You have been trying to defeat temptation through promises you repeatedly break.
You have been fighting resentment with forced smiles.
You have been trying to heal wounds by refusing to acknowledge that they exist.
And then, when you fall, you assume that Jesus must be disgusted with you.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Gospel says that our hope does not begin with how strong we are.
It begins with what Christ has accomplished.
And to see that clearly, we must go back to an earlier chapter of the same letter.
Paul writes that God raised Christ from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places:
“Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come.” — Ephesians 1:21, KJV
There it is again.
Principality.
Power.
Dominion.
But this time, the emphasis is not on the enemy.
It is on the exalted Christ.
Jesus is above them all.
Not struggling to become victorious.
Not anxiously waiting to discover whether darkness will defeat Him.
Not negotiating with the powers of evil over who possesses ultimate authority.
He is enthroned above every rule and authority.
The same letter that warns us about spiritual opposition begins by declaring the supremacy of Jesus Christ over every power.
That is not a coincidence.
That is the foundation of Paul's entire teaching about spiritual warfare.
And it gets even more beautiful.
In Ephesians 2, Paul describes humanity's former condition apart from Christ.
He speaks of people walking according to the course of this world, under the influence of the ruler of the authority of the air, and living in disobedience.
But he does not stop there.
Two words interrupt the darkness.
“But God.”
“But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us...” — Ephesians 2:4, KJV
Those two words carry enough hope to reach into the deepest scandal of your life.
But God.
You were lost.
But God.
You were enslaved to sin.
But God.
You had no righteousness of your own to offer Him.
But God.
You had a history that you could not undo.
But God.
And because of His mercy, Paul says that God made us alive together with Christ.
Not because we earned resurrection.
Not because we finally became respectable.
Not because we successfully hid everything shameful about ourselves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Do you see the connection?
Paul does not teach spiritual warfare as a separate fascination disconnected from salvation.
He places it within the great story of God's redemption.
The same Christ who rescues sinners is the Christ who strengthens His people against evil.
The same grace that saves us is the grace that teaches us to stand.
And this is where the enemy's accusations become so cruel.
Because one of the most painful battles a believer can experience is the battle over identity.
You know what you did.
You know what you said.
You remember the choices that nearly destroyed your marriage, your family, your reputation, or your relationship with God.
Maybe nobody else knows.
Maybe you have spent years carrying the consequences.
Maybe you still remember the night you crossed a line you swore you would never cross.
And sometimes the memory comes back without warning.
In the middle of worship.
During prayer.
When you are finally beginning to feel peace.
A thought rises:
Who do you think you are?
After what you did?
You think God really wants you?
Now, not every condemning thought is necessarily a direct demonic communication. Human memory, guilt, trauma, temptation, and patterns of thinking also matter.
But Scripture does identify Satan as an accuser.
Revelation 12:10 calls him the accuser of God's people.
And this accusation is answered not by pretending sin is harmless, but by the victory of Christ.
Because the Gospel never says your sin was insignificant.
It says Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The cross is not God overlooking evil.
It is the place where the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Repentance is not denial.
Forgiveness is not permission to continue harming others.
Grace is not the cancellation of accountability.
But neither is your worst moment the final authority over your identity when you belong to Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “redemption” is ἀπολύτρωσιν (apolytrōsin).
It speaks of release or liberation, a term associated with redemption.
In Ephesians 1:7, Paul connects this redemption directly with the blood of Christ and the forgiveness of sins.
You cannot purchase that redemption with religious performance.
You cannot earn it by punishing yourself emotionally for the rest of your life.
And no spiritual power can overturn what God has accomplished through His Son.
This does not mean a Christian will never struggle again.
It means the struggle takes place under the lordship of a victorious Savior.
And now Paul's command in Ephesians 6 begins to make sense.
“Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.” — Ephesians 6:11, KJV
The word translated “wiles” is μεθοδείας (methodeias).
It refers to schemes or crafty methods.
Paul uses the same Greek noun in Ephesians 4:14 when warning against the craftiness of deception.
That connection is worth noticing.
Because the enemy's schemes are not limited to dramatic displays of evil.
Deception matters.
False teaching matters.
Distorted desires matter.
A lie believed long enough can reshape the way a person lives.
Consider how temptation often works.
It rarely begins by announcing the full cost.
It begins with a suggestion.
You deserve this.
Just this once.
Nobody will find out.
You can repent afterward.
God understands.
And when the sin has done its damage, the message changes.
You are disgusting.
You will never change.
God is finished with you.
First, sin is made to look harmless.
Then grace is made to look impossible.
That is a devastating pattern of deception.
And whether we are confronting spiritual temptation, our own sinful desires, or the pressures of a broken world, the answer is not to negotiate with lies.
It is to return to the truth of God.
This is why Paul describes the armor of God in terms of truth, righteousness, readiness associated with the Gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, and prayer.
These are not magical objects.
They are not formulas for controlling spiritual forces.
They describe the resources God provides for His people to remain faithful.
Think about the first piece.
“Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth...” — Ephesians 6:14, KJV
Truth.
Not speculation.
Not fear.
Not rumors about demons.
Truth.
The truth of God's character.
The truth of His Word.
The truth of what Christ has accomplished.
The truth about our sin and our need for repentance.
The truth about the forgiveness available through Jesus.
The truth that we do not need to invent a false version of ourselves to be loved by God.
Some of you are exhausted because you have been trying to maintain an image.
At church, you are the strong one.
At home, you are falling apart.
Online, you post verses about peace.
At night, you cry because your heart is full of anxiety.
People call you faithful.
But privately, you feel like a fraud.
And you have become so accustomed to saying, “I'm okay,” that you no longer know how to tell someone the truth.
But listen.
God does not ask you to defeat darkness by becoming a better actor.
He calls you to walk in the light.
That may mean confessing sin.
It may mean asking someone to pray with you.
It may mean seeking wise pastoral counsel.
It may mean receiving professional help for emotional or psychological suffering.
It may mean admitting that you need protection from someone who has been harming you.
None of those things makes you less spiritual.
Truth is not the enemy of faith.
And a church that understands spiritual warfare should never make suffering people afraid to seek appropriate care.
Then Paul speaks of the breastplate of righteousness.
And we must remember the larger message of Ephesians.
Our standing before God is rooted in His saving grace through Christ, not in our ability to make ourselves righteous.
Yet the life of a redeemed believer must also reflect that grace through genuine obedience.
God does not save us by good works.
He saves us for good works.
Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
So when temptation invites you back into darkness, remember that grace is not merely the forgiveness of your past.
Grace also calls you into a transformed way of living.
You do not have to keep feeding the sin that once enslaved you.
You can confess.
You can turn away.
You can seek accountability.
You can remove access to the things that repeatedly lead you into temptation.
And when you stumble, you can return to Christ in repentance rather than running deeper into secrecy.
This is not effortless.
Sometimes obedience feels like losing something you desperately want.
Sometimes forgiveness requires surrendering the fantasy of revenge.
Sometimes faithfulness means walking away from a relationship you wanted to keep.
Sometimes repentance means making restitution and accepting consequences.
But the call of Jesus is not to decorate the old life with religious language.
It is to follow Him.
And following Him changes how we fight.
Paul speaks next about having our feet prepared with the Gospel of peace.
Peace.
What an unexpected word in a passage about warfare.
Yet it fits the whole letter.
In Ephesians 2:14, Paul declares concerning Christ:
“For he is our peace...”
He is speaking particularly about how Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles, creating one reconciled people through His cross.
That context matters.
Because one of the great works of darkness is division.
Hatred.
Hostility.
Pride.
The conviction that certain people are beyond the reach of mercy.
But Jesus came to reconcile sinners to God and to create peace among those who belong to Him.
So how tragic would it be if Christians used Ephesians 6 as an excuse to hate the very people they are called to love?
Your battle is not against flesh and blood.
That includes the people who disagree with you.
That includes the people who do not yet believe.
That includes the family member who has wandered far from God.
You may confront lies without despising the person deceived by them.
You may oppose injustice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
You may defend the truth without abandoning the character of Christ.
The Gospel does not call us to become cruel in the name of spiritual warfare.
It calls us to stand firm in a world that desperately needs the truth and love of Jesus.
Then Paul writes:
Imagine those flaming arrows.
Fear.
Doubt.
Temptation.
Accusation.
Despair.
The sudden thought that God cannot be trusted.
The whisper that obedience is pointless.
The crushing belief that your prayers no longer matter.
Faith does not mean pretending those arrows are not painful.
Faith means entrusting yourself to the God who remains faithful when your emotions are trembling.
Sometimes faith sounds triumphant.
Sometimes faith sounds like a broken person whispering:
Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Those words come from Mark 9:24.
And they remind us that a person can bring an imperfect, struggling faith to Jesus.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive spiritual performance before approaching Him.
You need Him.
Perhaps tonight your faith feels smaller than it did five years ago.
Perhaps grief has shaken you.
Perhaps you prayed for someone who died.
Perhaps you believed your marriage would survive, but it did not.
Perhaps you have begged God for healing, and the pain remains.
I will not insult your suffering by promising that every hardship will disappear if you simply believe hard enough.
Paul himself knew suffering.
He knew persecution.
He knew weakness.
He knew what it meant to depend upon the grace of God in circumstances he could not control.
And Scripture never promises that every faithful believer will experience immediate deliverance from every earthly difficulty.
But it does promise that nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
The shield of faith is not confidence that life will always go your way.
It is confidence in the God who remains worthy of trust when life does not.
And then comes the helmet of salvation.
Imagine a believer who has spent years hearing the voice of shame.
You are what you did.
You will always be that person.
Your past has already decided your future.
But salvation announces that the final word over the redeemed does not belong to shame.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
Not because we are innocent of every accusation.
But because our Savior is merciful, righteous, and mighty to save.
The Christian hope is not self-reinvention.
It is redemption.
It is being brought from death to life by the grace of God.
It is having a new identity in Christ that produces a new direction of life.
And that is the heart of Gospel Warrior's message.
Not because scandal is glamorous.
Not because sin is something to celebrate.
Not because the consequences of our choices disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose stories seem hopelessly ruined.
Consider the apostle Paul himself.
Before he became a missionary proclaiming Christ, he persecuted the church.
He approved of violence against believers.
He tried to destroy the very movement he would later serve.
If you had known him before his encounter with Jesus, you might have concluded that he was the last person God would use to proclaim the Gospel.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him.
Paul's past was real.
The harm he had caused was real.
But God's mercy was real too.
And the man who once persecuted Christians became a witness to the grace of the Savior he had opposed.
That is not a story about how good Paul was.
It is a story about how merciful Jesus is.
And if you are reading this while carrying the weight of a shameful past, do not confuse the seriousness of your sin with the impossibility of forgiveness.
Come to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from what is evil.
Receive His mercy by faith.
And begin walking in the new life He gives.
Then Paul describes the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God.
Notice that the armor passage gives believers one weapon explicitly described as a sword.
And it is not anger.
It is not political power.
It is not intimidation.
It is the Word of God.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered with Scripture.
He did not need to invent spectacular rituals.
He responded to temptation with the truth of what God had spoken.
And Christians today need that same deep familiarity with Scripture.
Not isolated verses twisted into promises God never made.
Not sensational interpretations that turn every headline into a secret prophecy.
Not teachings that make believers dependent upon personalities who claim exclusive knowledge of invisible spiritual realms.
We need the Word of God understood in context.
We need the whole counsel of Scripture.
We need to know who Jesus is, what He has accomplished, what He commands, and what He promises.
Because a Bible sitting unopened on a shelf will not shape your thinking the way a Bible faithfully read, believed, and obeyed can.
And perhaps one of the quietest tragedies of modern Christianity is that some believers know more about the latest controversy than they know about the words of Christ.
They can recognize the language of spiritual warfare.
But they are unfamiliar with the Sermon on the Mount.
They can discuss demons for hours.
But they struggle to explain the Gospel.
They are quick to identify darkness in the world.
But slow to confess pride, greed, lust, dishonesty, and bitterness in their own hearts.
Yet Paul does not call us merely to recognize evil.
He calls us to stand in God's strength.
And then, almost as though he refuses to let us mistake spiritual warfare for self-reliance, he tells us to pray.
“Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit...” — Ephesians 6:18, KJV
Prayer is not an afterthought.
It runs through the believer's life of dependence upon God.
And there is something deeply moving about what Paul says next.
He asks believers to pray for him.
For boldness.
For the ability to proclaim the mystery of the Gospel.
Think about that.
The man writing about principalities and powers does not ask the church to help him become famous for defeating demons.
He asks for prayer so that he can faithfully proclaim Jesus Christ.
At the time of writing, he describes himself as an ambassador in chains.
His circumstances are painful.
His freedom is restricted.
Yet his concern is that the Gospel would be declared boldly.
That should reshape the way we understand spiritual warfare.
The battle is not about making ourselves appear powerful.
It is about remaining faithful to Jesus in the face of evil, temptation, suffering, deception, and opposition.
And there is another passage that brings the entire picture into sharper focus.
Colossians 2:15 says that through Christ's triumph, the rulers and authorities were disarmed and publicly exposed.
Christ's victory over the powers is connected to His saving work.
The cross, which looked like defeat to those watching, became the place where God's redemptive purpose was accomplished.
The One who was mocked as King is the risen and exalted Lord.
The One who wore a crown of thorns is worthy of every crown.
The One who was nailed to a Roman cross is the One before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
This is the great reversal at the center of Christianity.
The apparent triumph of darkness did not prevent the resurrection.
The grave did not hold Jesus.
And the powers of evil do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
But be careful not to misunderstand what that means.
The New Testament still calls believers to resist the devil.
It still warns about temptation.
It still teaches vigilance.
It still acknowledges suffering and persecution.
Christ's decisive victory does not mean that the present conflict has already disappeared.
It means the outcome of God's redemptive purpose is secure in Him.
And this is why Paul repeatedly uses the language of standing.
Stand.
Withstand.
Stand firm.
Not because Christians are invulnerable.
Not because we are incapable of failure.
But because God has supplied what His people need to remain faithful in the conflict.
Sometimes standing looks like refusing a temptation when nobody would have discovered your compromise.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it looks like getting out of bed after grief has made ordinary life feel impossible.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of spiritual dryness.
Sometimes it looks like saying, “Jesus, I need You,” when you have no eloquent prayer left.
And sometimes standing looks like returning to the Savior after you have fallen.
Not excusing the fall.
Not pretending it did not matter.
But refusing to let shame drive you farther away from the only One who can restore you.
There is a reason the Gospel is such good news.
Jesus did not come merely to give strong people a few additional religious tools.
He came to save sinners.
He came to seek and to save the lost.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
And He calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is the message at the center of everything.
Not demons.
Not fear.
Not human personalities.
Not spiritual sensationalism.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And perhaps you have reached this point in the article realizing that the greatest battle in your life right now is not the one you have been talking about publicly.
It is the one you have been hiding.
The addiction you keep returning to.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The compromise you keep justifying.
The secret dishonesty.
The spiritual numbness.
The resentment toward God because life has not turned out the way you expected.
Or perhaps your struggle is simply that you are tired.
So tired.
You still believe.
But the joy feels distant.
You still pray.
But your words feel empty.
You still attend church.
But you wonder whether anyone would notice how much you are hurting if you stopped pretending to be strong.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Your exhaustion does not surprise Jesus.
Your tears do not embarrass Him.
Your questions do not make Him less sovereign.
And your need for help is not proof that you have failed as a Christian.
Bring your struggles into the light.
Seek the support of trustworthy believers.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Receive the help you need.
And keep turning toward Christ.
Because the answer to spiritual warfare is not a life controlled by fear of darkness.
It is a life increasingly rooted in the Lord who has overcome it.
And that brings us to one final truth from Ephesians that we cannot afford to miss.
Paul's letter is not addressed merely to isolated individuals fighting private battles.
It is addressed to the church.
A people joined together in Christ.
A people called to unity.
A people instructed to speak truth, put away bitterness, forgive one another, walk in love, reject darkness, and live as children of light.
Spiritual warfare is not meant to turn Christians into lonely warriors who distrust everyone around them.
It should drive us toward deeper dependence on Christ and faithful life together as His people.
We need Scripture.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need accountability.
We need fellowship.
We need the encouragement of believers who will remind us of God's truth when our own hearts are weary.
And that is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell the grace of God.
Not to make anyone feel that spiritual growth can be purchased.
But to help put Christ-centered biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources within reach of people who genuinely want to grow.
These resources are intended to help you read, reflect, learn, and strengthen your understanding of Scripture.
And if this article has helped you see Ephesians 6 more clearly, please do not let it end as another post you read and forget.

Not because a saved article possesses spiritual power, but because there may come a day when fear returns, temptation presses harder, or shame begins speaking again, and you need to remember what Scripture actually says.
Somebody who follows you may be fighting a battle they have never had the courage to discuss.
Someone may be blaming every hardship on demons while overlooking the hope of the Gospel.
Someone may have stopped praying because they believe their past has made them unworthy of God's mercy.
And I want to ask you something more personal.
Not for a performance.
Not to pressure you into making a public confession.
But because sometimes the beginning of change is the moment we stop pretending.
What battle has been hardest for you lately?
Fear?
Temptation?
Shame?
Bitterness?
Spiritual exhaustion?
You can simply write, “I'm still fighting, but I'm holding on to Jesus.”
You do not need to disclose private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss publicly.
But if you need encouragement, let the community know.
Someone reading may need to be reminded that God's grace is not just a doctrine written on a page.
It is the grace that saves and transforms real people.
There is also another way to stand with this ministry.
And it should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe.
The New Testament teaches generosity that is willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, service, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
These items are not spiritual necessities.
They are simply practical resources and expressions of appreciation for those who choose to stand with the ministry.
And the free resources are there because the truth of God's Word should never be treated as a privilege reserved only for people who can afford a monthly payment.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical teaching with someone who needs it matters.
Your faithfulness to Jesus matters.
Because this entire message began with one frightening reality.
We are not wrestling merely against flesh and blood.
There are principalities and powers.
There is spiritual opposition.
There is deception.
There is a real enemy who opposes God's purposes.
But the letter that warns us about the powers of darkness also announces something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ has been raised from the dead.
He is seated above every principality and authority.
Through His blood, sinners receive redemption and forgiveness.
Through grace, the spiritually dead are made alive.
Through His Spirit, believers are strengthened.
Through His Word, they are equipped.
And through His mighty power, they are called to stand.
So tonight, if you are afraid, look to Christ.
If you are tempted, turn to Christ.
If you have sinned, repent and come to Christ.
If you are wounded, bring your pain to Christ and seek the help and care you need.
If you are exhausted, do not mistake your weakness for the absence of His strength.
And if you have spent years believing that your story ended when your life fell apart, remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the persecutor who became an apostle.
Remember the sinners who were welcomed by the Savior.
Remember that Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
The powers of darkness are real.
But they are not ultimate.
Your past is real.
But it does not have to be your master.
Your wounds are real.
But they do not make you unreachable.
Your battle is real.
But Jesus Christ is Lord.

And one day, the conflict that has exhausted God's people for generations will finally give way to the fullness of His kingdom, when evil is judged, death is defeated, and God's redeemed people dwell with Him.
Until that day, we do not live in terror.
We stand in the Lord.
We cling to His truth.
We walk in His grace.
We proclaim His Gospel.
And we remember that the One who calls us to stand is the same Savior who gave Himself to bring us home.
